cards.h: 1. Risk aversion is best read from the utility curve
cards.b: Every R1-R8 row is expected-value neutral, so the ladder reveals a pattern rather than a degree. Two respondents switch part way, at R4 and R3, which is precisely what prospect theory predicts. We therefore estimate risk aversion from the utility curve, where it is sharply identified.

cards.h: 2. We extended the instrument to capture loss aversion
cards.b: Each V1-V6 row is a double-or-nothing gamble, so the certain amount cancels and the row reveals curvature. We added a mixed gain-and-loss gamble, which places the two limbs on a common scale and delivers lambda, the central parameter of prospect theory.

cards.h: 3. Three value rows measure one parameter, so we report its reliability
cards.b: All three imply the same curvature. Roll 251250039 answered 0.40, 0.45 and 0.70, implying 1.32, 1.15, 0.51. Reporting the spread of 0.81 alongside the mean of 1.00 turns a hidden error into a measured one.

cards.h: 4. The return assumption moves the answer more than the client does
cards.b: Both respondents with a complete utility curve want more than 100% equity under every input set, so the no-borrowing cap sets the allocation. The live question is how much of the 24.9% Problem Statement 1 return to carry forward.

slides.title: Method and Data Notes

cards.b: Prefer certain X if u(w0+X) > 0.5 u(w0+2X) + 0.5 u(w0). By Jensen's inequality this holds at every X or at none, so the switch point is read as a pattern.
U(A) = 0 and U(B) = 1, so U(X) = p at indifference. Fitted with the lecture's log form and a CRRA form; the CRRA coefficient is the A used in Step 5.
At indifference v(X) = p v(2X), so alpha = -log2(p). The certain amount cancels, which is what makes each curvature cleanly identified.
Maximise U = E(r) - 0.5 A sigma^2 along the capital allocation line: y* = [E(rP) - rf] / (A sigmaP^2), with borrowing capped at zero.

card.h: The cap, not the preference, sets the answer
card.b: Both respondents with a complete curve would borrow, so both are advised to hold 100% of their corpus in the Problem Statement 1 portfolio: Rs 90,000 and Rs 10 lakh. Volatility is carried across untouched because it is the reliable half of the estimate.

slides.foot: Adding these four turns the safety and potential split from a judgement into a measurement, and they take about a minute to answer.

card.h: Personality shapes the process, not the weight
card.b: Risk aversion is already measured directly, so personality is used where it actually predicts: whether a client stays with the plan.

cards.b: Conscientiousness of 2.33. Automate the contribution, rebalance on a threshold, and fix review dates in advance.
Conscientiousness 3.83, the group's lowest negative emotionality at 1.67, and the certain amount on all eight rows. A glide path that steps equity up over time suits this well.
Balanced across every domain. The switch at R3 suggests risk is judged in nominal amounts, so the downside case lands better as a rupee figure than as a percentage.
Chose the gamble throughout and preferred cash now at every rate offered. A short interview will establish the real horizon before the plan is set.

slides.title: The Robo-Advisory Portal
slides.lead: A single static page with no server and no sign-in, so it opens on a phone in a classroom.

cards.b: All six class sections plus the four extensions, written in plain English, with autosave and a one-click export of each respondent's answers.

The mean-variance allocation and the behavioral layers, against the real Problem Statement 1 frontier, with commentary generated from the respondent's own scores.
